body.text: Attribution: Sunaina Kumar and Soumya Bhowmick, “Jobs, Growth, and Market Access: Can India’s FTAs Be More Inclusive?” ORF Issue Brief No. 897, Observer Research Foundation, September 2026.

India’s free trade agreements (FTAs) now carry greater developmental expectations. While they primarily remain instruments for market access, tariff reduction, customs simplification, and commercial expansion, they are also being asked to foster job creation, strengthen small firms, broaden women’s economic participation, and make integration into global value chains (GVCs) more socially productive. This marks an important shift in India’s trade policy, where the question is no longer only whether FTAs expand trade, but whether they expand access to the gains from trade.

This broader shift is not unique to India. The 2024 report, Trade and Inclusiveness: How to Make Trade Work for All, argued that amid geopolitical tension, contested globalisation, widening inequality, technological disruption, and climate change, decades of trade-led growth have left some economies and many groups within them on the margins, held back by tariffs, weak regional integration, poor infrastructure, and weak institutions.[1]

The pattern is sharper in Asia and the Pacific, which accounts for roughly one-third of the GVC trade. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) finds that gains have been uneven both across and within economies, with smaller firms and women concentrated in lower-paid, less-protected, and often informal roles, even as competitiveness shifts from cost towards standards compliance and digital capability.[2] This is also where trade policy meets sustainable development: decent work, gender equality, support for small enterprises, and reduced inequality all depend on who can participate in trade and share in its gains. In response, recent FTAs have started housing these concerns in dedicated trade and sustainable development chapters, leading to a steady rise in inclusiveness-related provisions over the past three decades (see Figure 1).
Source: World Trade Organization[3]

Note: This figure shows the evolution of provisions on inclusiveness in RTAs between 1990 and 2021. The inclusiveness RTA index ranges from 0 to 1 and considers 33 explicit types of provisions addressing different dimensions of inclusiveness, including human rights, workers, MSMEs, poverty, gender, indigenous communities, persons with disabilities, and other minorities and vulnerable groups. “North” is defined as high-income economies, whereas “South” is defined as low- and middle-income countries, according to the World Bank’s income group classification (2022).

India's recent FTAs reflect this transition, albeit unevenly. The 2022 India–Australia Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (ECTA) mentions sustainable growth only in its preamble,[4] while the 2022 India–United Arab Emirates (UAE) Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) includes chapters on small and medium enterprises and on economic cooperation, both referring to sustainable and inclusive growth.[5] Later agreements go further. The 2024 India–EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) contains a trade and sustainable development chapter covering employment, gender equality, and climate change;[6] the India–Oman CEPA, in force since June 2026, links market access to inclusive growth and sets out cooperation on skills, digital transformation, agriculture, renewable energy, and healthcare.[7] The India–United Kingdom (UK) Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), in force since 15 July 2026, goes furthest, with dedicated chapters on small and medium enterprises (SMEs) (19), labour (20), environment (21), trade and development cooperation (22), and trade and gender equality (23).[8] The European Union (EU)–India FTA, concluded in January 2026 and still subject to legal revision, includes chapters on SMEs (12), sustainable food systems (15), and trade and sustainable development (16).[9] The New Zealand–India FTA, signed in April 2026, concluded but not yet in force, includes chapters on sustainable development (12), economic cooperation (14), and SMEs (15).[10]

This brief focuses on two areas significant for India's long-term growth: the micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSME) economy and women's economic participation. These are central to the inclusiveness agenda, as they represent one of India's largest pools of underutilised economic potential and operate in sectors with immediate FTA-linked demand, where market access, jobs, and a fairer distribution of gains meet. Drawing on literature review, secondary data analysis, and sector-specific research, the brief examines how greater integration of smaller firms, women, and informal workers into international trade can expand employment and economic opportunities. It aims to contribute to the broader objectives of SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) by recommending pathways to inclusive and sustainable trade-led development.

The Economic Survey 2025–26 identifies MSMEs as central to India’s industrial transformation: they account for 35.4 percent of manufacturing, 48.58 percent of exports, and 31.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), and include over 74.7 million enterprises employing more than 328.2 million people. Additionally, the survey links MSMEs to supply-chain participation, local value addition, and inclusive regional growth. On women’s work, it notes that female labour-force participation rose from 23.3 percent in 2017–18 to 41.7 percent in 2023–24, while female-headed proprietary establishments increased from 24.2 percent in 2021–22 to 26.2 percent in 2023–24.[11]

Despite these developments, India’s MSMEs and women workers remain unevenly integrated into the GVCs. MSMEs’ strong aggregate export share does not automatically translate into participation in higher-value segments, as smaller firms continue to suffer from limited access to trade finance, weak digital readiness, standard compliance costs, and inadequate export information. Similarly, there remains a stark gender gap: fewer than 5 percent of working women participate in trade and trade-related services, compared to nearly 15 percent of working men.[12]

India’s recent FTAs create market-access opportunities in labour-intensive and MSME-intensive sectors such as textiles and apparel, gems and jewellery, processed foods, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, leather and footwear, marine products, and horticulture. These sectors are therefore important channels through which trade gains could reach smaller firms and women workers, provided the implementation addresses barriers related to finance, certification, market information, and buyer-network access.[13]

The alignment between FTA market access and MSME-intensive sectors also creates an important policy opportunity, allowing India to not only unlock export growth but also distribute its benefits to economically marginalised segments. However, realising this potential requires deliberate institutional action.

MSMEs are central to India’s economic transformation, yet their integration into GVCs remains uneven. Their large contribution to manufacturing, exports, and employment has not translated into equally strong access to preferential export opportunities under recent FTAs. The disconnect between trade preferences and their utilisation reveals a critical implementation gap. While tariff reductions create legal opportunities for exports, smaller firms often cannot absorb the compliance costs, navigate complex rules of origin, access working capital, meet technical standards, or obtain the necessary certifications.[14]

The reasons these barriers affect smaller firms the most are well established in the empirical literature on preference utilisation. While the financial benefits an FTA offers scale with a firm’s export value, the cost of accessing them remains largely the same. Proving origin, obtaining certificates of origin, meeting technical standards, and gathering market intelligence are fixed costs, whether a consignment is worth US$5,000 or US$5 million. Thus, the utilisation of tariff preferences rises with export volume, which is typical of a fixed rather than a variable cost of compliance. Firm-level evidence shows that larger firms are better able to comply with rules of origin than smaller ones.[15]

India’s own utilisation record illustrates the scale of the gap, though only partially. The country’s overall FTA preference utilisation has historically hovered at around 25 percent, as against 70–80 percent in developed economies, with wide variation across agreements; utilisation under the India–Australia ECTA has been reported at 84 percent.[16] Under the India–UAE CEPA, about 240,000 certificates of origin were issued in the Agreement’s first three years, covering US$19.87 billion in preferential exports, a fraction of India’s total merchandise exports to the UAE over the same period.[17] None of these figures, however, is disaggregated by firm size. India publishes utilisation in aggregate value terms, so whether the gains are broadly shared or concentrated among a small number of large exporters is not public knowledge. Until utilisation data are disaggregated by firm size, claims about MSME participation in FTA gains, positive or negative, cannot be verified, making the monitoring measures recommended below a precondition for evaluating the rest.

India’s recent FTAs have begun addressing these barriers through dedicated MSME chapters and trade facilitation commitments, although implementation remains inconsistent. First, the India–UAE CEPA has produced visible trade-scale effects, with bilateral trade rising to US$100.06 billion in FY 2024–25, a 19.6 percent increase.[18] Its implementation framework has prioritised rules of origin, customs facilitation, and technical requirements—issues critical to MSME participation. However, public evaluation of MSME-specific gains remains limited; without firm-size-disaggregated export data, it is difficult to assess whether smaller Indian exporters have benefited from these gains proportionately.

Second, the India–Australia ECTA provides Indian exporters near-complete tariff advantages in the Australian market. Australia offers duty elimination on 100 percent of its tariff lines for imports from India: 98.3 percent became duty-free immediately, while the remaining 1.7 percent are to be phased to zero over five years.[19] India’s offer to Australia is more selective. However, whether MSMEs are able to use these preferences depends on logistics costs, certification requirements in regulated sectors, and information gaps about rules of origin and claim procedures. [20]

Third, the India–EFTA TEPA represents a more integrated approach to MSME-relevant support. Beyond tariff concessions, it combines trade facilitation, investment-promotion commitments, standards cooperation, regulatory dialogue, and a Trade and Sustainable Development chapter.[21] Its institutional mechanisms, including committees and sub-committees on trade facilitation and sustainability, can be used to identify and address standards, certification, and information barriers faced by smaller exporters.

MSMEs often struggle to secure export finance because of collateral, documentation, and audited accounts requirements. Furthermore, firms in tier-2 and tier-3 cities face gaps in digital infrastructure, e-commerce integration, and digital literacy.[22] Certification and testing requirements in markets such as the EU, UK, and Australia impose fixed costs that are often unaffordable for smaller firms.[23] The key policy lesson is that tariff concessions alone cannot deepen MSME integration into global markets. FTAs must be backed by soft financing, targeted capacity-building, cluster-level testing facilities, and trade facilitation systems designed for smaller exporters. The India–EFTA TEPA is instructive here, as its committees and sub-committees on trade facilitation and sustainability can, if used actively, be directed towards these firm-level barriers.

These constraints fall even harder on women, who are clustered in many of the same labour-intensive sectors yet remain furthest from trade's rewards. International trade can transform women's lives by creating better jobs, raising wages, opening pathways to higher-skilled work and entrepreneurship, and reducing economic inequalities.[24] Research by the World Bank and the World Trade Organization (WTO) has shown that gains from trade are higher for women in developing countries, firms that are part of GVCs tend to employ more women, and jobs in GVC-integrated sectors are more likely to offer higher pay and benefits than those in firms not directly engaged in trade.[25] In India, less than 5 percent of working women participate in trade and trade-related services such as transport, logistics, and customs clearance.[26]

Despite the potential of trade to enhance gender equality, trade and gender became more institutionalised at the WTO only in the late 2010s and early 2020s, with the WTO’s current Action Plan on Trade and Gender covering 2021 to 2026.[27] Many trade agreements now include gender-specific provisions. The WTO’s 2022 database on gender provisions in RTAs identified 331 gender provisions across 109 RTAs, covering issues such as women’s economic participation, entrepreneurship, labour conditions, access to productive resources, unpaid care work, and safety.[28] A comprehensive mapping of these provisions finds that cooperation-based clauses (information exchange, capacity-building, and best-endeavour commitments) remain by far the most common type, while binding obligations are rare.[29]

In the last decade, India has concluded several important trade agreements, with gender provisions appearing in the India–UAE CEPA, India–EFTA TEPA, India–UK CETA, India–Oman CEPA, and the EU–India FTA.[30] The India–UK CETA represents the most explicit attempt to embed gender within India’s FTA architecture. Rather than treating women’s inclusion as an indirect outcome of trade expansion, the Agreement includes a dedicated “Trade and Gender Equality” chapter focused on enhancing opportunities in both countries for women workers, business owners, and entrepreneurs to participate in global, regional, and domestic economies. It acknowledges barriers that limit women’s economic participation—including unpaid care work, limited access to finance, skills gaps, digital exclusion, weak trade networks, and the absence of gender-disaggregated data—and commits to strengthening the competitiveness of women-led enterprises by advancing skills, capacity-building, information and technology, financial inclusion, market access, and trade finance.[31] It also establishes a Trade and Gender Equality Working Group, comprising government representatives from both countries, to support implementation, monitor progress, and report through the Agreement’s institutional structure once it enters into force.

However, inclusion written into an agreement does not automatically translate into inclusion in export markets. An International Trade Centre study identifies unrealised Indian export potential of approximately US$3.9 billion under the India–UK CETA alone, spanning apparel and textiles, gems and jewellery, electronics and machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, and horticulture and processed food.[32] However, the same study cautions that women’s participation in these gains cannot be assumed, as they often remain concentrated in production while being excluded from export management, buyer negotiations, formal finance, certification systems, and international networks. The policy challenge, therefore, is not simply whether CETA expands trade, but whether women-led enterprises and women workers are positioned to avail of the opportunities it creates (see Table 1).
Table 1: India–UK CETA and Women’s Trade Participation

Both the India–UK CETA and the EU–India FTA texts create significant opportunities in labour-intensive sectors, such as textiles, garments, leather and footwear, marine products, gems and jewellery, and tea and spices. Since these sectors employ a high concentration of women, expanding them directly impacts women’s jobs, incomes, and pathways into formal employment. However, to fully unlock this potential, trade facilitation measures must specifically target women-owned enterprises, particularly given the barriers women face in navigating complex export procedures, accessing customs regulations, and meeting documentation requirements.[35]

In the EU–India FTA text, gender provisions are incorporated in the Trade and Sustainable Development chapter, including commitments to promote gender equality; support gender-disaggregated data collection and gender-based analysis of trade policies; promote women-run MSMEs and agribusinesses; support women-led enterprises, cooperatives, and collectives; and expand business development services, financial inclusion, vocational training, export finance, venture capital, microfinance, and women’s engagement in digital trade.[36] Unlike the India–UK CETA, however, the EU–India text does not include a standalone chapter or a dedicated working group. Its effectiveness will, therefore, depend on how the wider trade and sustainable development and institutional mechanisms are used during implementation.

Labour-intensive, MSME-dominated sectors have a greater capacity to absorb female labour, since they require lower capital investment and offer more flexible, informal entry than capital-intensive industries. Therefore, the barriers examined—compliance costs and technical standards for MSMEs; unpaid care work, digital exclusion, and weak trade networks for women—cannot be viewed separately. This overlap informs the recommendations, highlighting the need for intersectional policy responses to support MSMEs and women’s economic participation.

The discussion so far has treated MSME and gender provisions as commitments whose main deficiency lies in delivery. However, this framing is incomplete: the inclusiveness agenda is contested terrain, and India has long been among its critics. At the WTO’s Singapore Ministerial Conference in 1996, members designated the International Labour Organization (ILO), not the WTO, as the competent body for labour standards; explicitly rejected the use of such standards for protectionist ends; and affirmed that the comparative advantage of low-wage developing countries should not be called into question.[37] India has long viewed gender provisions in trade agreements with similar suspicion, and its recent embrace of them marks a deliberate change of course.[38]

However, scholars caution that most such provisions remain largely symbolic, unless matched by implementation capacity and resources.[39] For instance, a standard can act as a size filter even when its content is benign, since a compliance requirement that a large firm absorbs as a routine cost can be prohibitive for a micro enterprise. Consider the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which entered its definitive phase on 1 January 2026. Affected goods made up close to a tenth of India’s exports to the EU in 2022–23, with an estimated average additional burden of around 25 percent.[40] Exporters unable to produce verified emissions data must use default values that carry a mark-up—a penalty that falls frequently on MSMEs, which lack such monitoring, reporting, and verification capacity.[41] The EU Deforestation Regulation similarly placed a disproportionate burden on smaller operators and had to be postponed twice, with a later deadline for micro and small enterprises—an acknowledgement that the burden falls by size.[42]

It also matters whether a provision is cooperation-based or enforcement-based. Many MSME and gender provisions are cooperation-oriented and rely on dialogue, capacity building, and review, with their legal character differing across agreements. The India–UK CETA expressly bars either party from taking any matter under its gender chapter to dispute settlement (Article 23.5).[43] The India–EFTA TEPA’s sustainability chapter carries an equivalent carve-out with a periodic review, while the agreement as a whole must be reviewed two years after its entry into force.[44] The now-concluded EU–India text keeps its sustainability chapter outside binding dispute settlement. Enforcement-based provisions,[45] which the EU has pursued since 2022 by linking sustainability commitments to dispute settlement and sanctions, appear in no agreement India has signed.[46] The enforceable pressure on Indian exporters therefore comes from autonomous partner regulation rather than FTA texts; the EU–India FTA delivered no CBAM exemption, only 500 million euros for sustainable industrial transformation and a technical dialogue on emissions methodologies.[47]
The value of the cooperation chapters lies in their potential to be channels for compliance capacity and the recommendations in this brief are framed accordingly.

India’s recent FTAs mark an important shift in trade policy design. MSME and gender provisions are no longer peripheral add-ons; they are increasingly becoming part of the architecture of inclusive trade. However, the presence of such provisions in legal texts does not automatically translate into meaningful access for smaller firms, women-led enterprises, or workers in vulnerable sectors. Tariff preferences and market-access commitments must be accompanied by institutional support, affordable finance, digital facilitation, certification infrastructure, skills development, and regular monitoring. Without these complementary measures, FTAs risk reinforcing existing inequalities as larger firms with stronger networks, better access to finance, and greater compliance capacity are more likely to capture the gains from liberalisation.

The policy challenge, therefore, is to move from agreement design to implementation capacity. Trade facilitation, export finance, skills development, MSME support, and women’s economic empowerment currently sit across different ministries, departments, and financial institutions. This fragmentation weakens follow-through and limits the ability of FTAs to generate inclusive outcomes. To address this, India must build stronger accountability structures, publish granular data, and connect market access with targeted capability-building.

The following recommendations provide a pathway for making India’s FTAs more operationally inclusive. They are not of equal weight: robust monitoring, the second recommendation, is a precondition—until utilisation and participation data are disaggregated by firm size and ownership, none of the other measures can be evaluated. The third and fourth recommendations target the two largest fixed costs identified in this brief—documentation and standards compliance—and should be prioritised. The remaining measures build on these foundations.

Create dedicated implementation cells within the Department of Commerce to coordinate MSME and gender provisions across FTAs. These cells should have designated officials, budgets, timelines, and reporting obligations, and should convene relevant ministries, export-promotion councils, state governments, standards bodies, and financial institutions. Rather than exercising open-ended regulatory powers, their primary function should be to coordinate implementation, identify bottlenecks, and publish progress updates.

Establish standardised metrics to track MSME participation in exports under each FTA by firm size, sector, and state, and women’s participation by enterprise ownership, employment, and export value. These indicators should feed into annual implementation reviews published openly. While current FTA reviews focus largely on aggregate trade volumes, granular MSME and gender data can enable mid-course corrections and evidence-based learning. The India–UK CETA, with its dedicated chapter and working group on trade and gender equality, can serve as an early pilot.[48] Much of the required data already exists: since January 2025, preferential certificates of origin have been filed through the Directorate General of Foreign Trade’s eCoO 2.0 common digital platform, which links each application to the exporter’s Importer-Exporter Code. The Udyam registration, in turn, links these codes to firm-size categories.[49] Cross-tabulating the two would enable a quarterly firm-size-disaggregated utilisation dashboard without requiring new surveys.

Prioritise paperless trade infrastructure in MSME-intensive sectors and export corridors, including textiles, processed foods, marine products, gems and jewellery, and pharmaceuticals. This initiative should be aligned with the National Trade Facilitation Action Plan (NTFAP) 3.0, which advances India’s “Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) Plus” agenda.[50] Additionally, the government should establish an implementation benchmark for faster digital processing of MSME shipments under FTA rules, supported by district-level help desks, cluster-level training, and state-level digital trade facilitation centres in major export clusters.

Establish joint testing and certification facilities in high-export zones, such as Tamil Nadu for apparel, Maharashtra for chemicals and pharmaceuticals, Gujarat for agri products, and Kerala or Andhra Pradesh for marine products. These facilities should be co-funded by the central government, state governments, and sector industry associations. Certification costs should be subsidised for MSMEs and women-led enterprises, especially in sectors where technical, sanitary, phytosanitary, environmental, or sustainability standards are central to market access. Since the EU’s CBAM and Deforestation Regulation now make emissions and traceability data a prerequisite for market access, these facilities should also provide monitoring, reporting, and verification support. Furthermore, India should lobby to channel the EU’s 500 million euro industrial-transformation commitment towards these facilities.
5. Expand Access to Trade Finance for Women-Owned Msmes

Work with the Export–Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank), the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI), and state-level finance institutions to design export credit lines for women-led MSMEs with reduced collateral requirements, risk-sharing or guarantee cover, grace periods aligned with production cycles, group guarantee options, and capacity-building embedded in credit terms. These instruments should address systemic barriers such as collateral requirements, digital divides, and financial literacy gaps.

Future FTAs should include Trade and Gender Equality Working Groups, drawing from the India–UK CETA model.[51] These groups should be empowered to monitor gender provisions, recommend operational adjustments to implementation agencies, engage women’s business associations and MSME chambers, and publish annual progress reports. Representation must include women-led enterprises and grassroots MSME networks, in addition to government officials. Scheduled review processes and working group meetings should be used to assess implementation and identify gaps. For example, the India–EFTA TEPA permits a review of its trade and sustainable development chapter two years from entry into force, and the India–UK CETA requires the Trade and Gender Equality Working Group to meet within a year of entry into force. India should enter both with a costed capacity-building agenda and published indicators, ensuring the best-endeavour commitments secure budgets and reporting lines.

FTA implementation should be connected more closely with India’s skills ecosystem, including sector skill councils, state skill missions, and industry-led training platforms. Priority should be given to green skills and standards-related training in sectors covered under recent FTAs, including renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, food processing, textiles, and manufacturing. The government must set phased annual targets for MSME workers, including women workers, to receive green-skills certification in FTA-relevant sectors.

The recommendations outlined in this brief highlight the central challenge: tariff liberalisation alone cannot ensure inclusive trade; MSMEs and women-led enterprises require the institutional conditions needed to capitalise on the opportunities created by FTAs. This means access to affordable finance, simplified compliance systems, digital infrastructure, testing and certification support, transparent data, and sustained engagement with women’s business associations and MSME networks. The India–EFTA TEPA’s combination of market access, trade facilitation, and sustainability institutions offers a useful template; however, the institutions involved must be equipped to address firm-level barriers.[52]

In India’s context, inclusive implementation is also how trade agreements deliver on their sustainable development commitments. The trade and sustainable development chapters cover both MSME and gender provisions, and labour and environmental standards, with mutually reinforcing benefits. For instance, drawing smaller firms and women into sectors such as renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and food processing advances decent work, gender equality, and lower inequality while supporting the green transition. Treating inclusiveness and sustainability as a single, unified agenda thus gives India's FTAs a clearer purpose beyond market access.

Expanding trade without addressing unequal access to finance, information, technology, and standards-compliance capacity can risk widening existing divides. However, if implementation is designed around inclusion, FTAs can become instruments not only of market access but also of enterprise upgrading, women’s economic participation, and regional export diversification. Sectors such as apparel, jewellery, processed foods, electronics, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, and sustainable agriculture offer clear opportunities for MSMEs and women entrepreneurs. Realising these gains will require institutional innovation, sustained political commitment, and a shift from legal commitments to operational delivery.
